items.label: f03-null-unique
items.front: Why must StockMovement rows carry orderId for @@unique([orderId, productId, reason]) to stop double restocks?
items.back: PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct in unique indexes, so (NULL, productId, 'RESERVE') rows never collide. Write movements after tx.order.create so the order id exists.

items.label: f02-assert-loser-wrote-nothing
items.front: In a stale-version test, which assertion do juniors leave out?
items.back: Re-read the stored row and assert the loser wrote nothing. A 409 status alone would not catch a repository that returns 409 after having written the row.

items.label: f01-invariants-first
items.front: Name this order system's invariants before reading any controller.
items.back: Stock is never negative; a pending order restores its stock at most once; an order's price comes from the server catalog; historical item prices do not change when the catalog changes.

items.label: f04-debounce-vs-cache-key
items.front: Out-of-order search responses: debounce timer or cache key?
items.back: The cache key. A timer changes when requests are sent, not which response wins; with ['products', { search, offset }] a response for one search cannot be written into another's entry. Reset offset in the same update that changes search.

items.prompt: A cart has two products. The first reservation succeeds and the second has insufficient stock. What happens to the first product's stock?

choices.text: It stays decremented until the order is cancelled
It stays decremented: an admin has to restock it by hand
Partial order: the first product ships alone, the second is back-ordered
It is restored: the 409 rolls back the entire transaction

choices: It stays decremented until the order is cancelled
It stays decremented: an admin has to restock it by hand
Partial order: the first product ships alone, the second is back-ordered
It is restored: the 409 rolls back the entire transaction

items.explanation: Atomicity is about all related writes; the suite even injects a failure at the final order insert to prove reservations alone do not commit.

items.prompt: In the idempotent-create sketch, two requests with the same key both miss the key lookup. Why does the loser usually report 'Inventory changed' instead of returning the existing order, and what is the fix?

choices.text: The fingerprint differs between concurrent requests; hashing the body fixes it
PostgreSQL deadlocks on the two rows; retrying the whole transaction fixes it
It blocks on the winner's row lock and fails the version check before any key insert; lock the key first
The unique key insert fails first; catching every exception as a duplicate fixes it

choices: The fingerprint differs between concurrent requests; hashing the body fixes it
PostgreSQL deadlocks on the two rows; retrying the whole transaction fixes it
It blocks on the winner's row lock and fails the version check before any key insert; lock the key first
The unique key insert fails first; catching every exception as a duplicate fixes it

items.explanation: The loser waits on the winner's product row lock, then fails the version clause before it reaches the key insert; the fix is to serialize on the key (an advisory lock) before the lookup. Keep a P2002 handler only as a backstop and catch only that code; catching every exception turns a connection failure into a wrong 200.

choices.text: The interactive transaction, which runs the two requests one after another from the start
The JavaScript check, because the second request sees the updated stock
The conditional updateMany, whose stock filter is evaluated inside the write itself
A unique constraint on order items per product

A unique constraint on order items per product

items.explanation: The JavaScript comparison is a courtesy check for a friendly message; both requests pass it. The guarantee is the where clause evaluated at the write boundary.

items.prompt: Cancellation restores stock with an unconditional increment. What can go wrong given that validation caps editable stock at 2,000,000,000?

choices.text: Stock silently wraps around to a negative number in the database
Nothing goes wrong: the increment is clamped to the validation cap inside the update
The cancellation fails with 409, like in the ecommerce project, and stock stays put
Stock can pass the cap, and then saving the unchanged edit form fails validation with 400

choices: Stock silently wraps around to a negative number in the database
Nothing goes wrong: the increment is clamped to the validation cap inside the update
The cancellation fails with 409, like in the ecommerce project, and stock stays put
Stock can pass the cap, and then saving the unchanged edit form fails validation with 400

items.explanation: A restore can push stock past the 2,000,000,000 cap, after which saving the unchanged edit form fails validation with 400: every writer of a column must respect the same bounds. The ecommerce sibling refuses such a cancellation with an explicit 409; here the restore has no upper bound.

choices.text: db is not connected inside a transaction callback, so the write throws
db writes are rejected by the unique index while tx is open
A db write commits on its own and would survive a rollback of the order
tx writes are faster, and ledger rows are written in bulk

db writes are rejected by the unique index while tx is open
A db write commits on its own and would survive a rollback of the order
tx writes are faster, and ledger rows are written in bulk

items.explanation: The stock delta and its explanation must commit together; a ledger that writes outside the transaction can fail or succeed independently.

items.prompt: Transactions keep the data consistent. What do they NOT establish in this project?

choices.text: Authorization: callers supply userId and CORS accepts every origin
Price history: order items keep the price that was paid at checkout
Atomicity: every reservation loop either applies whole or not at all
Non-negative stock: the conditional decrement never lets it drop below 0

choices: Authorization: callers supply userId and CORS accepts every origin
Price history: order items keep the price that was paid at checkout
Atomicity: every reservation loop either applies whole or not at all
Non-negative stock: the conditional decrement never lets it drop below 0

items.explanation: Authorization: userId is caller-supplied and CORS accepts every origin, so any local client can cancel or fulfill any order id. Data consistency, identity and delivery uncertainty are different concerns; a retried POST can also create a second order because idempotency is not implemented.

items.prompt: A product has 100 in stock and two customers each buy one unit concurrently. Why can the second get 409 'Inventory changed during checkout'?

choices.text: PostgreSQL detects a deadlock between the two transactions and aborts the second
Both read version 3 without a lock, so T2's version clause then matches nothing
The stock clause gte 1 fails once the first unit is sold to the other customer
It cannot: with 100 in stock both orders succeed every time

choices: PostgreSQL detects a deadlock between the two transactions and aborts the second
Both read version 3 without a lock, so T2's version clause then matches nothing
The stock clause gte 1 fails once the first unit is sold to the other customer
It cannot: with 100 in stock both orders succeed every time

items.explanation: stock gte alone already prevents overselling, and the version increment in data protects stale editors, so the version in the where buys little and costs real orders.

items.prompt: Checkout sorts cart lines with localeCompare; cancellation walks items ordered by the database. Why is that a review point?

choices.text: localeCompare is too slow for large carts and stalls checkout under load
Mixed-case or punctuated ids could make the two paths lock rows in opposite orders
Cancellation should not lock product rows, since it only adds stock back
The database ignores orderBy inside a transaction, so the order is random

choices: localeCompare is too slow for large carts and stalls checkout under load
Mixed-case or punctuated ids could make the two paths lock rows in opposite orders
Cancellation should not lock product rows, since it only adds stock back
The database ignores orderBy inside a transaction, so the order is random

items.explanation: With ids whose collation differs from localeCompare (mixed case, punctuation), checkout and cancellation could take row locks in opposite orders; one plain comparison everywhere removes the question. With Prisma cuid() ids both orders agree today, but consistent lock order should not depend on two different sort rules.
